newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-EUROPE MUST AVOID BATTLE OVER WORLD CUP, GERMANS SAY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-EUROPE MUST AVOID BATTLE OVER WORLD CUP, GERMANS SAY.

text.p: German soccer chiefs said on Monday that they were pleased that Europe's governing body UEFA was backing their bid to host the 2006 World Cup and not England's, because the continent had to avoid a bitter battle at all costs.

German soccer federation (DFB) spokesman Wolfgang Niersbach admitted the DFB had been surprised by the fax which UEFA sent to the English Football Association (F.A.) on Friday confirming its support for the Germans.

The English called the decision undemocratic. But Niersbach said it was important because Europe did not want the kind of costly squabbling that marred the contest for the 2002 tournament between Asian rivals Japan and South Korea.
The tournament was eventually awarded jointly to the bitter regional rivals.

"Look at the millions that were spent on that battle in Asia," Niersbach said. "We think it is good that UEFA has made its position clear... We respect the English bid but we want them to respect our bid."
"The UEFA fax took us by surprise at the weekend. But we have known since 1993 that we had backing when (FIFA president Joao) Havelange said he would be in favour of Germany.

"(UEFA president) Lennart Johansson was there when he said it...All the major countries in Europe have had the World Cup and major tournaments in recent years. We knew it was our turn. That is why we put our bid in early."

The Germans have been talking about a bid for the 2006 World Cup for several years. At the 1994 World Cup national coach Berti Vogts often expressed his concerns that the country needed to work hard on its youth players now if it wanted to be successful at the event on home soil.
But the DFB's assumption that Germany is due a major international event is shaky.

Niersbach said all Europe's other major football countries had hosted events recently, citing the 1990 World Cup in Italy, France's hosting of the next finals in 1998 and the European championship in England last year.

But the fact is England have not held the World Cup since 1966 while Germany last held the finals in 1974. Although England did host Euro 96, it is not long since Germany had the continent's top tournament, hosting Euro 88.
The DFB stressed it did not want a battle with the English over the UEFA fax.
"It is going to be hard enough to get the finals here (in Europe)," Niersbach said. "People are talking about the 'old Krauts' but we were not involved in any of this."

The UEFA decision is almost certainly going to be a big talking point in Britain in the next few months with a general election looming. Political campaigners often see a nationalistic issue like hosting a sports event as a vote winner.
Niersbach said the UEFA fax might have been sparked by British prime minister John Major's plans to host a reception soon at Downing Street for delegates from the world governing body (FIFA).
